name: Alkaline water / alkaline diet

lead: The alkaline diet and alkaline water are based on the idea that what you eat or drink shifts body pH. The diet favours fruit and vegetables and excludes most grains, meat, cheese and eggs, and followers say it brings clearer skin, more energy and less bloat.

Proponents say foods leave acidic or alkaline residues that affect the body. Reviews and physiologists report that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH in healthy people, which is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45, and no appearance studies were found.

paras: People eat mainly fruit and vegetables and cut animal foods and grains, and some drink water made with ionizer machines or take alkalizing supplements. Followers typically describe it as a long-term eating style.
Excluding food groups can cause nutrient deficiencies, and cancer organisations caution against relying on it for treatment. Ionizers and supplements add cost, and promoters often sell them.

angle.text: Followers of the alkaline diet and alkaline water say they improve skin, energy and general health by shifting body pH. The diet's emphasis on fruit and vegetables is conventional eating advice, while blood pH is tightly regulated and appearance effects have not been shown in studies.

lead: The alkaline diet is a group of loosely related eating patterns built on the idea that foods leave acidic or alkaline residues that shift the body's pH. It favours most fruit and vegetables and limits grains, meat, cheese and eggs. Alkaline water, often made with ionizer machines or sold bottled at a raised pH, is promoted on a similar premise.[1][2]

People adopt these approaches hoping for a clearer, glowing complexion, slower visible aging, a leaner body and more energy. The plant-heavy diet overlaps with eating patterns that are widely encouraged for general health, and Wikipedia notes that the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics review found elements such as eating green leafy vegetables likely healthy.[1]

The theory itself is contested: reviews report that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH in healthy people, which is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45.[1] Research on alkaline water has examined athletic and metabolic outcomes rather than appearance.[3][4][5]

paras: Versions of the diet differ, but most rank foods by supposed alkaline or acid-forming effect and encourage the alkaline group. Promoters such as Robert O. Young, author of The pH Miracle, have offered it as a route to weight loss, according to Wikipedia; Lalita Kaul's review for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics found parts of it likely healthy while concluding that its reliance on fasting and supplements makes it not a healthy way to lose weight.[1]

Marketers of ionized water say it can slow aging, offset acidic foods or hydrate better after exercise.[2] A 2022 review of electrolyzed-reduced water argued that observed effects of such water are explained by dissolved molecular hydrogen rather than by alkalinity or other proposed properties.[6]

In the 1800s Claude Bernard observed that rabbits switched from plants to meat produced more acidic urine, and later researchers burned foods and measured leftover ash, leading to the dietary ash hypothesis. Alkaline diets were historically used to prevent kidney stones and urinary infections.[1]

A 2013 review by Hanley and Whiting found no evidence that diet changes blood pH or bicarbonate in healthy people, and urine pH is reported not to reflect overall body acidity.[1] A systematic review in BMJ Open found no link between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer, and several cancer organisations reject the cancer claim.[2]

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics said parts of the diet such as eating green leafy vegetables are likely healthy, while the British Dietetic Association criticised it in 2018.[1] Excluding food groups can risk nutrient deficiencies, and cancer patients are cautioned about extreme diets.[1]

No studies found testing alkaline water or the alkaline diet for skin or appearance outcomes. A 2017 review of ten studies on dietary acid load and exercise found that lower acid loads raised plasma pH but did not consistently improve performance, while suggesting a more alkaline dietary pattern may suit overall health.[3] A 2024 trial in 22 trained athletes combined an alkalizing diet with bicarbonate-rich water or placebo over a simulated three-day 400 m race.[4] A 2024 randomised trial in boxing athletes examined alkaline water with L-glutamine and reported higher salivary alpha-amylase and testosterone concentrations.[5] A 2025 pilot trial examined electrolysed alkaline water in hyperuricemia.[7]

lore.intro: Alkaline eating and water appear in training and wellness forums as part of detox and cleansing routines.[8]
